concept.name: Time value
concept.definition: That portion of an option's premium that exceeds its intrinsic value; it reflects the probability that the option will move (further) into the money before expiration, so the longer the time remaining, the greater the time value, all else equal.
concept.intuition: Time value is the price of possibility: with more days left, there is more chance for the underlying to move in your favor, and the market charges for that chance.
concept.mechanics: Time value = premium - intrinsic value. It decays as expiration approaches (theta decay), with decay accelerating in the final weeks and being most pronounced for at-the-money options; higher implied volatility raises it, and it reaches zero at expiration.
concept.formula: Time value = option premium - intrinsic value.
concept.failure_modes: Long-option positions lose time value every day even when the underlying is flat, so a correct directional view can still lose money if the move comes too slowly; decay is nonlinear, so linear extrapolation of daily decay underestimates late-life erosion.
concept.misconceptions: Time value does not measure how much time is left in a literal sense — two options with identical time to expiry can have very different time values because volatility and moneyness differ.
concept.example: A two-week $32.50 call on a $32.80 stock priced at $1.10 has $0.80 of time value; at expiration, if the stock is still $32.80, the premium collapses to roughly its $0.30 intrinsic value.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
